svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Private Google Access for on-premises hosts works in Google Cloud and how it differs from the VM version; on-premises hosts reach Google APIs over Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect, and the subnet flag that the VM version depends on is explicitly not needed here, so everything is DNS, firewall rules and routes instead; on-premises hosts must connect through the virtual IP addresses for either the restricted or private googleapis.com domains rather than the ordinary API addresses; the mechanism that makes it private is that Google publishes DNS A records resolving those domains to a VIP range but publishes no routes to that range, so you add a custom advertised route on a Cloud Router and a custom static route in the VPC network whose next hop is the default internet gateway, and traffic stays on Google's network because no external routes exist; the allowed source addresses being private RFC 1918 addresses or privately used public addresses but never a Google-owned public address, and any IPv6 global or unique local address except one reserved range; the two DNS approaches, either on-premises name servers resolving the domains directly or a Cloud DNS private zone reached through an inbound server policy whose forwarder entry point must be in the same region as the tunnel or VLAN attachment; the return path constraint that the next hop tunnel or attachment must be in the region where the request originated or the response never arrives; and the wildcard override trap where only APIs supported by the chosen VIP remain reachable and Cloud DNS cannot do partial overrides
svg.title: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts: no subnet flag, all routing and DNS
svg.text: Same product name, almost nothing in common with #90.
The subnet flag is not merely unnecessary here — the documentation says so outright.
The sentence that resets your expectations
“YOU DON’T NEED TO ENABLE PRIVATE GOOGLE ACCESS FOR ANY SUBNETS IN YOUR VPC NETWORK as you
would for Private Google Access for Google Cloud VM instances.”
Instead: DNS, firewall rules and routes — in BOTH your on-premises and VPC networks.
Why it is private, in three steps
1. Google PUBLICLY publishes DNS A records resolving the VIP domains to a VIP range.
2. Even though those ranges hold EXTERNAL addresses, Google publishes NO ROUTES to them.
3. So YOU supply the routing: a CUSTOM ADVERTISED ROUTE on a Cloud Router, plus a CUSTOM
STATIC ROUTE in the VPC network whose NEXT HOP is the default internet gateway.
Result: traffic stays on Google’s network, because no external route to it exists.
You must go through a VIP — on-premises hosts have no other door
Connect via the VIPs for EITHER restricted.googleapis.com OR private.googleapis.com. Which
one you pick decides what is reachable: services are limited to those the domain supports.
(The ranges, protocol limits and record shapes are #92’s subject.)
Allowed SOURCE addresses
• A private address, e.g. RFC 1918
• A privately used PUBLIC address —
but NEVER a Google-owned one
• Any IPv6 GUA or ULA, except one
reserved ULA range
Re-using Google public IPs: unsupported
Two ways to do the DNS
A. On-premises name servers resolve the
domains to the VIP range themselves
B. A Cloud DNS private zone, reached by
an INBOUND SERVER POLICY, with
on-prem forwarding to an inbound
forwarder entry point
… in the SAME REGION as the tunnel
The return path has a region constraint, and it fails silently in one direction
The next-hop Cloud VPN tunnel or VLAN attachment back to on-premises MUST BE IN THE SAME
REGION WHERE THE REQUEST ORIGINATED.
If it is in a different region, the RESPONSE WILL NOT REACH the on-premises network — the
request goes out fine. Classic one-way failure, and nothing reports it as a routing fault.
The wildcard override trap
Pointing all of googleapis.com at one VIP means ONLY THE SUPPORTED APIS ARE ACCESSIBLE,
“which might cause other services to be unreachable.”
And Cloud DNS DOES NOT SUPPORT PARTIAL OVERRIDES. If you need them, the docs say use BIND.
Everything this post needs, you already built
Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect (#85–89) → a custom advertised route on Cloud Router (#83)
→ a custom static route whose next hop is the default internet gateway (#90) → DNS you own.
No new primitives. This is six posts of plumbing pointed at one destination.
